ANIMAL CATEGORIES LESSON · ANIMAL CATEGORIES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Whales & Dolphins — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the ocean’s air-breathing giants, one spout at a time.

What is this?

Whales and dolphins are mammals, not fish — they breathe air with lungs, feed their babies milk, and must come up for breath, which is why they blow the famous spout.

What does it mean?

Mammal is the family word: hair (a little), milk, live babies, air to breathe — the ocean’s giants are our relatives, not the fish’s.

What does the child need to know?

The blue whale is the biggest animal that has ever lived; dolphins whistle name-like calls and sleep with half their brain awake; manatees graze seagrass like underwater cows; dugongs are the sailors’ "mermaids".

Why this matters

The biggest animal ever on one card, plus the mermaid mix-up — this is the deck’s easiest wow, and the ocean-conservation talk starts here.

What it teaches

Classification (mammal vs fish), size-scale wonder, and listening skills through whale-song play.

Words to learn

whaledolphinspoutmammalbreathmanateedugongseagrasscalfsong

Say this to your child

“"Whales and dolphins are mammals — like us! They breathe air and feed their babies milk. The whale’s heart is as big as a car, the dolphin whistles its own name, and the sea cows munch seagrass all day. Up for air — WHOOSH, the spout!"”

Step by step

  1. The mammal rule: whales and dolphins are not fish — no gills, lungs instead; no eggs, live babies; and milk for the calf.
  2. The spout: the breath made visible — warm air blasts out the blowhole when they surface. Count the spouts on a boat trip.
  3. The whale: the blue whale’s heart is the size of a small car, and its song travels across whole oceans.
  4. The dolphin: the whistler — each has a signature whistle, like a name. They call each other by it.
  5. The sea cows: the manatee and dugong graze seagrass meadows slowly all day; sailors who glimpsed them from ships wrote home about mermaids.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the whale arcs with its spout, the dolphin rides the wave, and the round-faced manatee and dugong drift below — the two sea cows side by side. Which one has the biggest mouth on the card?

Ask your child

"Is a whale a fish?" (no — a mammal, like us) "How does a dolphin have a name?" (a signature whistle) "Which two animals are the sea cows?" (the manatee and the dugong)

What your child can say or do

Your child might answer every phone call with a whale song, sign birthday cards from "the dugong", or correct the mermaid record: "sailors saw SEA COWS, actually."

Out in the real world

Whale-watching boats run on the US, Canadian and UK coasts — the spout is the first sighting. Manatee parks in Florida let families watch sea cows float; dugongs live off Australia.

Try it together

Whale-song telephone: two paper cups joined by string — hum a long whale note, the listener answers with their own. Then dolphin jumps between two cushions, and a manatee float on the rug, slow as seagrass.

Understanding check

Ask: "What comes out of the blowhole?" (air — the spout) "What do manatees eat?" (seagrass) "Are whales and dolphins fish?" (no — mammals)

This lesson pairs with the Whales & Dolphins flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animal Categories.
